turns.question: Reading through these chapters, some steps are flagged as required and others as recommended. Practically speaking, what's the difference in what we have to do?
turns.answer:
The USGS National Field Manual defines the two terms this way: "required" reflects USGS Water Mission Area policy, established on the basis of research or technical consensus and reviewed by water-quality specialists, and USGS field personnel are instructed to use required equipment and procedures as described in the NFM 【1】. Departing from a required procedure is allowed only if it is "independently quality assured and documented" 【1】.

"Recommended" items, by contrast, indicate that "there are several acceptable alternatives to a given procedure or equipment selection" 【1】. You choose among the recommended alternatives based on "referenced research and sound field judgment," and you must document the reasons for your selection 【1】. Departures from recommended procedures also must be independently quality assured and documented 【1】.

Practically: required steps are fixed policy you follow as written (or formally justify and document any departure), while recommended steps give you a menu of acceptable options where you pick and justify what suits your project. Note these definitions are USGS-specific; whether they bind your own work depends on whose protocols you're operating under.

The USGS National Field Manual defines the two terms this way: "required" reflects USGS Water Mission Area policy, established on the basis of research or technical consensus and reviewed by water-quality specialists, and USGS field personnel are instructed to use required equipment and procedures as described in the NFM 【1】. Departing from a required procedure is allowed only if it is "independently quality assured and documented" 【1】.

"Recommended" items, by contrast, indicate that "there are several acceptable alternatives to a given procedure or equipment selection" 【1】. You choose among the recommended alternatives based on "referenced research and sound field judgment," and you must document the reasons for your selection 【1】. Departures from recommended procedures also must be independently quality assured and documented 【1】.

Practically: required steps are fixed policy you follow as written (or formally justify and document any departure), while recommended steps give you a menu of acceptable options where you pick and justify what suits your project. Note these definitions are USGS-specific; whether they bind your own work depends on whose protocols you're operating under.

turns.question: And if a site just won't let us do the required one - no room for the gear, say - is it enough to note it in the log and move on?
turns.answer:
No — a log note alone isn't enough under the USGS rules. For a required procedure, a departure is permitted only if it is "independently quality assured and documented" 【1】. The same condition applies to modifications of recommended procedures 【1】.

So if site conditions force you away from a required method, the excerpt supports two things beyond just writing it down: the departure must be documented, and it must be independently quality assured — meaning someone other than the person making the departure reviews it, consistent with the manual's broader expectation that records "should be checked independently by a field partner and (or) data administrator" 【2】. The excerpt doesn't spell out the exact quality-assurance steps, so you'd need to check the full NFM chapter or consult a water-quality specialist for how to carry that out.

No — a log note alone isn't enough under the USGS rules. For a required procedure, a departure is permitted only if it is "independently quality assured and documented" 【1】. The same condition applies to modifications of recommended procedures 【1】.

So if site conditions force you away from a required method, the excerpt supports two things beyond just writing it down: the departure must be documented, and it must be independently quality assured — meaning someone other than the person making the departure reviews it, consistent with the manual's broader expectation that records "should be checked independently by a field partner and (or) data administrator" 【2】. The excerpt doesn't spell out the exact quality-assurance steps, so you'd need to check the full NFM chapter or consult a water-quality specialist for how to carry that out.
